frase_gancho.texto: Two animals that hold the universe in balance.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue straight ahead to the courtyard. There, beneath a single column that holds up an enormous roof, stands The Umbrella, the heart of the building.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before “Duality,” the mural that Rufino Tamayo painted in 1964 in the museum’s lobby: more than twelve meters long, with two animals facing each other. On the left, under a red dawn sky, a feathered serpent in green: Quetzalcóatl, light and life. On the right, against a night-blue sky with a moon and stars, a jaguar leaping with its jaws open: Tezcatlipoca, the night. This is not a battle with a winner. In Mesoamerica the world held together because opposites needed each other: day and night, life and death, heat and cold. Tamayo did not copy codices: he told the story with modern color and a rough surface, almost like an ancient wall.

guion_largo.texto:
If you had to sum up in a single image what you are about to see in this museum, it would be this one. The peoples of Mesoamerica believed that the universe was not a straight line but a balance in motion, made of pairs that oppose and complete each other. The Mexica took this to its highest level: in the beginning there was a divine couple, Ometecuhtli and Omecíhuatl, the Lord and the Lady of Duality, who lived in the farthest heaven and from whom everything else was born. “Ome” means “two.”

Rufino Tamayo understood it this way. He was born in Oaxaca in 1899, of Zapotec origin, and unlike other muralists of his generation, he preferred not to tell political stories with crowds of characters. He wanted to speak through symbols and color, and that is why here there are only two animals and a great silence between them. The museum commissioned the mural for its opening in 1964 and placed it in the lobby, where every visitor passes it before entering the halls.

Notice how the color works. The serpent is green and emerges from a red dawn sky, and its body curves gently. The jaguar is orange and seems to fall upon it, surrounded by a deep blue sprinkled with stars and a moon. They are opposite colors, and that is why they vibrate. Tamayo knew that complementary colors become more intense side by side. It is the same idea as the gods: they strengthen each other because they are not alike. Moreover, the jaguar was the animal of Tezcatlipoca, “Smoking Mirror,” and its spotted skin was read as a night sky full of stars.

Quetzalcóatl and Tezcatlipoca were rivals and brothers at the same time. In the legend told at Tula, Tezcatlipoca tricked Quetzalcóatl with a mirror and forced him to flee. When you reach the Toltec Hall, you will see why that story mattered so much. And in the Mexica Hall, the same tension appears in another way: Huitzilopochtli, the sun, defeats [Coyolxauhqui](mna_s06_coyolxauhqui), the moon, in a combat that is repeated every day.

There is another detail that makes this mural special. Over the years, Tamayo gathered an enormous collection of pre-Hispanic pieces and donated it to his hometown; today it is the Rufino Tamayo Museum, in Oaxaca. In other words, he did not paint this mural as a decorator, but as a collector in love with that world. And that Oaxacan root has an echo in this museum: in the Oaxaca Hall you will meet [Cocijo](mna_s07_urna_cocijo), the Zapotec god of rain, a relative of the [Tláloc at the entrance](mna_s00_monolito_tlaloc).

Before moving on, take a moment in front of the mural. First look at the animal that draws your attention most, and then notice how the other one balances it. Then try the exercise of looking for pairs, because from here on you will see them everywhere. The eagle and the jaguar. Day and night. Life and death. The masculine and the feminine. Water and fire. Every time you discover one, you will be reading the museum as its creators read it.

texto: Compare the colors on the two sides: red and green against blue and orange
Find the moon and the stars above the jaguar
Step closer to see the rough surface of the paint

texto.Culture: Rufino Tamayo (1899-1991), muralism and modern Mexican art
texto.Material: Vinylite on canvas mounted on a stretcher frame, with a marble sand texture
texto.Location: Left wall of the main lobby (entrance to the Jaime Torres Bodet Auditorium)

texto.pregunta: Myth: Tamayo’s mural shows a battle between Aztecs and Spaniards.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It shows Mesoamerican duality, two opposing forces that need each other: the feathered serpent (the day) and the jaguar (the night).
